So `text` is built from the input, and then a trailing newline is appended if not present. So `text` always ends with `\n`. Then `parse_block(ob, doc, text->data, text->size)` is called.

So the document buffer passed to `parse_block` always ends with `\n`. This means the sub-buffer passed to `is_codefence` can't be the last 3 bytes all spaces.

Wait, unless the OOB read is not `data[3]` but something else. Let me re-read the fix:

```c
/* looking at the hrule uint8_t */
if (i + 2 >= size)
        return 0;
c = data[i];
if (!(c=='~' || c=='`'))
        return 0;
```

The OOB read is `c = data[i]` when `i + 2 >= size`. For `i=3`, `size=3`: `data[3]` is 1 byte past the sub-buffer. For this to be caught by ASAN, `data[3]` must be past the full document buffer.

Hmm, but the document ends with `\n`. Let me reconsider whether the trailing newline is really always there.

Actually, wait. Let me reconsider. Maybe the OOB happens in a caller where the sub-buffer is NOT the last line, but the sub-buffer's `data[3]` happens to be past the end because of how the buffer is allocated. No, ASAN only catches reads past the allocated buffer.

Let me reconsider. Maybe the trailing newline is NOT appended in the case where the input is empty or... no.

Actually, let me reconsider. Let me re-examine: maybe the OOB happens when the sub-buffer is the last line and the document does NOT end with `\n` because the input already ends with `\n` but... no.

Wait. Let me reconsider the `parse_listitem` path. The document is `- ` + 3 spaces. With trailing newline: `-    \n` (6 bytes). beg=2, end=6, end-beg=4. Sub-buffer = `   \n`. i=3, data[3] = `\n`. In bounds.

But what if the document is `- ` + 3 spaces and the trailing newline is NOT appended because the input already ends with `\n`? Then the input is `-    \n` (6 bytes), same thing.

Hmm. Let me reconsider. What if the list item content is such that `end - beg` is exactly 3 AND the sub-buffer is at the end of the document? For that, `end` must equal `size` (the document size), and `beg = size - 3`. But the document ends with `\n`, so `data[size-1] = '\n'`. The sub-buffer would be bytes `[size-3, size-2, size-1]` = `[c, c, \n]`. For all 3 to be spaces, `data[size-1]` must be a space, but it's `\n`. Contradiction.

So the trailing newline prevents this. Unless the trailing newline is NOT appended.

Let me reconsider. Maybe the issue is that the OOB read happens in a caller where the sub-buffer is the last line WITHOUT the trailing newline. Let me look at `parse_fencedcode` line 2297 again. The sub-buffer is `data + line_start` with size `i - line_start` where `i` is the position of `\n`. So the sub-buffer is a line WITHOUT the newline.

If the fenced code content's last line is `   ` (3 spaces) and it's the last line of the fenced code, and the fenced code is at the very end of the document... but the document ends with `\n`. So the fenced code content would be `...   \n`. The last line `   ` is followed by `\n`. So `i` = position of `\n`, sub-buffer = `   ` (3 bytes). `data[3]` = `\n`. In bounds.

Hmm. Still in bounds.

Wait, let me reconsider. Maybe the trailing newline is NOT appended in some scenario. Let me check: what if the input is empty? Then `text->size == 0`, so no newline appended, and `parse_block` is not called. Not relevant.

Let me reconsider. Maybe the OOB happens because the sub-buffer is at the end of the document and the document does NOT end with `\n` in the sub-buffer context. 

Actually, wait. Let me reconsider the `parse_fencedcode` path. The fenced code content is extracted from the document. Let me look at how `parse_fencedcode` is called and what `data`/`size` it receives. Let me look at line 3579 (parse_block).
